title: The British theologians: regeneration first, then our act of faith
source_text: LXV. Caeterum conversionem prout immediatum opus Dei designat, dicunt esse qua Deus animos electorum suorum prius variis actibus gratiae suae excitatos & praeparatos, intima quadam, & mirabili operatione regenerat, & quasi de novo creat; infundendo spiritum vivificantem & omnes animae facultates novis qualitatibus imbuendo. Hanc vero conversionem, ex eorum sensu, sequitur, non tempore sed natura, nostra conversio actualis, Deo proliciente ipsum actum credendi & convertendi ex mutata voluntate, quo acta a Deo agit & ipsa, convertendo se ad Deum & credendo, hoc est, actum suum vitalem eliciendo. Addunt divinam illam actionem non laedere voluntatis libertatem, sed roborare: nec extirpare radicitus vitiosam resistendi possibilitatem; sed efficaciter & suaviter dare homini firmam obediendi voluntatem.
pass_a_gloss: LXV. Moreover conversion as it designates the immediate work of God, they say is that by which God regenerates the souls of his elect, first stirred up & prepared by various acts of his grace, by a certain inmost, & wonderful operation, & as it were creates them anew; by infusing the life-giving spirit & imbuing all the faculties of the soul with new qualities. But this conversion, in their sense, is followed, not in time but in nature, by our actual conversion, God drawing forth the very act of believing & of converting out of the changed will, whereby, moved by God, it acts itself too, by converting itself to God & believing, that is, by eliciting its own vital act. They add that that divine action does not hurt the freedom of the will, but strengthens it: nor roots out by the roots the vicious possibility of resisting; but efficaciously & sweetly gives to man a firm will to obey.
pass_b_english: Thesis LXV. Conversion in the sense of God's direct work, they say, is the work by which God, through an innermost and wonderful working, regenerates the souls of his elect, which various acts of his grace have already stirred and prepared, and as it were creates them anew, pouring in the life-giving Spirit and filling every faculty of the soul with new qualities.

In their view this conversion is followed, not in time but in order of nature, by our actual conversion: God draws the act of believing and turning out of the changed will, and the will, moved by God, then acts too, turning itself to God and believing, that is, producing its own living act.

They add that this divine action does not damage the will's freedom but strengthens it. It does not tear out by the roots the corrupt possibility of resisting, but effectively and gently gives the person a firm will to obey.
